notes: Permission to appeal refused; Wilkie J's solicitor negligence findings on authority, loss and causation held unarguable.

enrichment.short_title: Aisbitt v Conrathe: permission to appeal on solicitor negligence after JR withdrawal
key_facts: Miss Aisbitt instructed Coningsbys in judicial review proceedings against South Bank University after she was required to withdraw from a postgraduate diploma in Psychosexual Therapy.

Public funding was granted on counsel's advice of 65-70% prospects but later terminated; the judge found she instructed the solicitors to withdraw the JR, leading to a consent order with a lottery costs provision.
Wilkie J found breach of contract and negligence by the solicitors but awarded only nominal damages of £2 and ordered Aisbitt to pay 60% of the defendants' costs.
Aisbitt appealed on authority to withdraw, failure to inform her of the consent order, alleged JR within a negligence trial, and refusal of substantial distress damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from a solicitor negligence trial judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the judge was entitled to find express authority to withdraw survived coming off the record, no loss because JR prospects were negligible, and no causative link between medical condition and solicitors' failings.
enrichment.ratio: Coming off the court record does not deprive solicitors of authority to act where actual authority has been given and not revoked; in a solicitor negligence action the trial judge must assess what would have happened had the solicitors not been negligent, and nominal damages may be appropriate where prospects of success in the underlying claim were negligible.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors had authority to consent to withdrawal of the judicial review after coming off the record
Whether the judge erred in holding a judicial review within a professional negligence trial
Whether substantial damages for distress and injury to health should have been awarded
Whether the judge's findings on loss and causation were open to him
linked_authorities: Sharpe v Addison [2003] EWCA Civ 1189
Dixon v Clement Jones Solicitors [2004] EWCA Civ 1005
Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd [2003] 1 AC 32

notes: Licence not tenancy for M Sites; annual protected tenancy found for Chester Road advertising structure.

enrichment.short_title: Clear Channel v Manchester: licence or tenancy of advertising hoarding sites
key_facts: Clear Channel erected giant M advertising structures on 13 Manchester city centre sites under an unexecuted March 2001 draft agreement with Manchester City Council.
MCC terminated the arrangements and put the sites out to tender; Clear Channel claimed protected business tenancies under Part II of the 1954 Act.
The March 2001 draft expressly stated no tenancy was conferred and granted permission to erect displays on wider undefined sites rather than exclusive possession of concrete bases.
At Chester Road, Clear Channel erected a substantial fixed structure and paid rent from June 2002 under terms agreed in a July 2001 letter though no formal lease was executed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of declaratory proceedings on whether Clear Channel held licences or tenancies of advertising sites.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed for the M Sites (licence only); counterclaim dismissed for Chester Road Site where Clear Channel established an annual tenancy in occupation protected by the 1954 Act.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a grant is a licence or tenancy depends on substantive rights not labels; permission to place removable advertising structures on council land without exclusive possession of defined areas is a licence, but erection of a fixed structure with exclusive possession and rent may create a periodic tenancy even where formal documents were not executed.
legal_issues: Whether the March 2001 draft agreement created tenancies of the M Sites
Whether exclusive possession was intended over concrete bases or wider council land
Whether Clear Channel occupied the Chester Road Site for business purposes under section 23
Whether any tenancy was only a tenancy at will under Cardiothoracic and Javad principles

Cardiothoracic Institute v Shrewdcrest Ltd [1986] 3 All ER 633
Javad v Aqil [1991] 1 All ER 243
Graysim Holdings Ltd v P & O Property Holdings [1996] AC 329

notes: CPO challenge dismissed; Inspector and SoS reasons on Wembley regeneration land held adequate under Porter.

enrichment.short_title: RE International v SoS: Wembley CPO reasons challenge dismissed
key_facts: RE International UK Ltd owned about 1.7 hectares of derelict land near the new Wembley National Stadium subject to an LDA compulsory purchase order.
REI accepted the need for a pedestrian link and marshalling yards but objected to compulsory acquisition of the remainder of its land, offering instead to pursue its own redevelopment.
The Inspector recommended confirmation of the CPO, finding regeneration more likely under LDA single-ownership and expressing little confidence in REI's delivery capacity.
REI challenged the Secretary of State's confirmation solely on inadequate and unintelligible reasons regarding acquisition of land beyond the pedestrian link.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 23 Acquisition of Land Act 1981 application to quash confirmation of a compulsory purchase order.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Inspector's report and decision letter adequately addressed the compelling public interest for acquiring the balance of REI's land, with costs awarded to the Secretary of State but not the LDA.
enrichment.ratio: Decision letters and inspectors' reports must be read as a whole by informed readers; paragraphs addressing both the pedestrian link and wider land redevelopment can intelligibly support a finding of compelling public interest for compulsory acquisition of the whole site without specifying exact redevelopment dates.
legal_issues: Whether reasons for confirming the CPO in respect of REI's balance land were adequate
Whether the Inspector conflated the pedestrian link timetable with overall regeneration timing
Whether a compelling public interest existed beyond land needed for the Wembley Link
Whether viability and cross-subsidy findings precluded acquisition of the balance site
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter (No 2) [2004] 1 WLR 1953
Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council v Secretary of State [1995]

confidence.notes: Single ground of challenge and detailed reasons analysis; costs and permission rulings also clear.

notes: Freezing injunction continued for solicitor's fees; section 69 and PHA threshold met despite privilege and non-disclosure points.

enrichment.short_title: Hakendorf v Countess of Rosenborg: freezing order over matrimonial assets for solicitor fees
key_facts: Solicitor Mary Hakendorf acted for the Countess of Rosenborg in bitter matrimonial proceedings and delivered a final bill of about £78,582 after her retainer was terminated.
Royce J granted a without-notice freezing injunction and section 69 liberty to sue before the one-month bill period expired, fearing the Wife might settle with her husband to defeat fee recovery.
The Wife withheld a £4,000 instalment ordered under an A v A costs order and disputed the bill, alleging a contingency fee arrangement and reviving withdrawn misconduct allegations.
The Wife sought discharge of the injunction, arguing no asset dissipation risk, flawed cause of action, privilege breach and material non-disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Return date hearing on continuation of a freezing injunction and section 69 order obtained without notice.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction continued until trial; permission to withdraw and substitute amended bill granted; Wife's discharge application and indemnity costs claim refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 69 and freezing order thresholds require probable cause that the client may act to prevent payment of solicitor's costs; a solicitor suing a former client may disclose privileged material to the court necessary to establish that case analogously to Paragon Finance waiver principles; minor non-disclosure does not warrant discharge where no prejudice results.
legal_issues: Whether there was a real risk of asset dissipation or collusive settlement
Whether section 73 charging order was the appropriate remedy instead
Whether the cause of action on the amended bill was valid
Whether the solicitor breached legal professional privilege or materially non-disclosed on the ex parte application

Paragon Finance plc v Freshfields [1999] 1 WLR 1183

notes: Night flying consultation settled by agreement; Forbes J ordered each side to bear own costs.

enrichment.short_title: Richmond v SoS: night flying consultation costs after agreed settlement
key_facts: Richmond London Borough Council challenged a July 2004 consultation on night flying restrictions at Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted.
The claim focused on paragraph 7.9 of the consultation paper, alleging the Secretary of State had fettered discretion by treating ICAO noise certification data as decisive.
During the hearing the judge indicated the claimants' characterisation of paragraph 7.9 was not justified and invited agreement.
The parties agreed a stay on terms confirming the defendant may have regard to operational noise and not merely ICAO certification data when formulating restrictions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs application after substantive judicial review proceedings were resolved by consent during the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Each party ordered to bear its own costs; the agreed terms largely reflected the declaration originally sought by the claimants.
enrichment.ratio: Where judicial review proceedings are compromised after the court identifies a possible flaw in the claimant's case and both sides make concessions, it is inappropriate to award costs on the merits when the court has not heard full argument and cannot say which party would ultimately have succeeded.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 7.9 improperly fettered the Secretary of State's discretion on aircraft noise
Whether ICAO certification data must be the sole basis for operating restrictions
What costs order should follow a part-heard claim resolved by agreement

confidence.notes: Costs ruling is clear though substantive merits were not finally determined.

notes: Landmark PHA authority: civil not criminal standard applies to section 3 harassment injunctions.

enrichment.short_title: Hipgrave v Jones: civil standard of proof for PHA injunctions
key_facts: Joyce Hipgrave claimed neighbours harassed her in a series of incidents including door banging, threats and an Asda confrontation over about ten months.
HHJ Hamilton found harassment proved against the first defendant on five incidents and against the third defendant on two linked incidents.
The first and third defendants appealed contending the criminal rather than civil standard of proof should apply to PHA injunctions, analogising ASBOs under McCann.
The judge had granted injunctions restraining further harassment after finding profound psychological impact on the claimant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on point of principle as to standard of proof for injunctions under section 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; civil standard of proof with strictness appropriate to seriousness applies to PHA civil proceedings, not the criminal standard used for ASBOs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 PHA civil claims are a private remedy protecting individual rights unlike public ASBO proceedings; the civil balance of probabilities standard applies with strictness commensurate to seriousness, while proportionality and Convention balancing under Re S and Cream may limit any injunction granted even where harassment is proved.
legal_issues: Whether McCann criminal standard applies to PHA section 3 injunction applications
How Convention Articles 8, 10 and 11 affect PHA injunctions
Whether two incidents sufficed as a course of conduct for the third defendant
Whether apprehended breach claims require criminal standard of proof
index_terms: In re H standard of proof

Thomas v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 1233
Cream Holdings Ltd v Banerjee [2004] UKHL 44

notes: Negative EMS statement in landlord counter-notice held directory; appeal allowed on mandatory/directory analysis.

enrichment.short_title: 7 Strathray Gardens: EMS negative statement in collective enfranchisement counter-notice

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Tenants at 7 Strathray Gardens served a section 13 collective enfranchisement notice and the landlords served a counter-notice admitting the claim but omitting a required EMS statement.
2002 regulations required a counter-notice to state whether premises were within an approved estate management scheme under section 70; the premises were not.
The judge held the omission mandatory and invalidating, entitling the nominee purchaser to acquire on the tenants' initial notice terms at a substantially lower price.
The Court of Appeal held a negative statement where no EMS exists is directory only, not mandatory with invalidity as sanction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court holding landlords' counter-notice invalid for failure to state premises were not in an EMS area.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; failure to include a negative EMS statement does not invalidate an otherwise compliant counter-notice.
enrichment.ratio: Under Petch v Gurney principles the effect of non-compliance depends on legislative intention; requiring a negative statement that premises are not within a section 70 EMS is beneficial not essential machinery, and omission cannot invalidate the counter-notice though tenants may have a separate claim for wasted expenditure.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 4 of the 2002 Counter-notices Regulations is mandatory or directory
Whether a negative EMS statement can invalidate the landlord's counter-notice
Whether section 25 applies where a non-compliant counter-notice is served
Whether Article 1 Protocol 1 requires directory construction
linked_authorities: Burman v Mount Cook Land Ltd [2002] Ch 256
Petch v Gurney [1994] 3 All ER 731
Cadogan v Morris [1999] 1 EGLR 59
Cutler v Wandsworth Stadium Ltd [1949] AC 398

notes: VAT repayment interest at section 78 rates not 8%; section 35A and Community law claims rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Elite Mobile v Customs: VAT repayment interest at section 78 rates
key_facts: Customs wrongly set off about £5.25m of Elite's VAT credits against a disputed assessment and delayed repayment until judicial review pressure.
Elite received principal repayment in July 2004 but claimed interest at 8% under section 35A rather than lower section 78 VATA rates of about 2-3%.
Customs contended section 78 applied due to official error and that pending section 79 supplement proceedings temporarily displaced section 78 liability.
Elite also relied on Garage Molenheide BVBA v Belgium for Community law interest at a commercial rate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for interest on VAT repayment after principal sum paid, heard substantively on interest grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for 8% interest rejected; declarations that interest is payable at section 78 rates for the agreed periods; permission to apply for judicial review granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where section 78(2)(a) temporarily excludes section 78 interest because a section 79 supplement may be ordered, section 35A(3) may apply but the court should fix rates having regard to Parliament's section 78 prescription; Community law does not require a higher rate where section 78 rates are not materially unjust.
legal_issues: Whether section 35A(3) applies after principal VAT debt paid in JR proceedings
Whether section 78(2)(a) bars interest while section 79 supplement is undetermined
Whether Community law requires interest above section 78 rates
Whether Schedule 11 VATA independently creates an interest obligation

notes: Insurance appeal dismissed; declaration 5 covered corporate insolvency; waiver obiter.

enrichment.short_title: Doheny v New India Assurance: non-disclosure of corporate insolvency on proposal form
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Doheny signed insurance proposal forms declaring no director or company in which they had an interest had been bankrupt or subject to bankruptcy proceedings.
After a fire, insurers denied cover because Mr and Mrs Doheny had been directors of three companies that entered liquidation between 1991 and 1994.
The judge preferred the insureds' narrow construction of declaration 5 as applying only to individual bankruptcy but held corporate insolvencies were materially non-disclosed.
The Court of Appeal held declaration 5 in common commercial parlance covered corporate insolvency as well as individual bankruptcy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judgment for insurers on fire claim denied for breach of proposal declaration and non-disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; breach of declaration 5 established and insurers entitled to avoid the policy; waiver argument obiter considered but not decisive.
enrichment.ratio: Where a proposal declaration asks whether any company in which a director had an interest has been declared bankrupt or subject to bankruptcy proceedings, those words in a business insurance context encompass corporate liquidation and insolvency, not only strict legal bankruptcy of individuals.
legal_issues: Construction of declaration 5 on bankruptcy of companies versus individuals
Whether corporate liquidations were material facts requiring disclosure despite specific questions
Whether insurers waived further disclosure by asking focused insolvency questions
Application of MacGillivray waiver principles to business insurance

notes: Summary judgment largely granted on voyage charter repudiation; clause 20 time bar rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Odfjell v CDPI: voyage charter repudiation damages and clause 20 time bar
key_facts: Owners chartered BOW CEDAR to carry jet fuel, gasoline and gas oil from Bahrain to Benin for US$825,000 lump sum freight under an amended BPVOY4 form.
Charterers cancelled on 2 September 2002 for failure to procure cargo; owners accepted repudiation and claimed about US$475,000 damages after mitigation voyage.
Charterers sought to amend defence to rely on clause 20 time bar requiring claims within 180 days of completion of discharge.
No cargo was ever loaded or discharged after laytime expired and demurrage accrued before termination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court summary judgment application under CPR Part 24 with proposed amendment to plead contractual time bar.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment largely granted; clause 20 did not bar damages claim where no discharge occurred; permission to amend time bar defence refused; conditional permission to defend on voyage length quantum only.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 20.2 time bar applies strictly to claims for amounts for charterers' account under the charter, not general damages for repudiation; where discharge never occurs and Hague-Visby Article III rule 6 expressly addresses non-delivery but clause 20 does not, no term can be implied that time runs from when discharge should have occurred.
legal_issues: Whether clause 20.2 covers damages claims for repudiation and failure to furnish cargo
Whether to imply a commencement date when no cargo discharged
Whether accrued demurrage before termination is recoverable as damages
Construction of laytime commencement where free pratique granted after six hours
